Chapter 3. The System of Dehumanization and the Erosion of Identity
The machinery of Auschwitz wasn’t just about concrete and steel. It ran on something far more chilling—a system designed to break the human spirit. Every single part of camp life was set up to strip people of their individuality, reducing them to nothing more than numbers.
Think about it: the identical uniforms, the shaved heads, the endless roll calls. All constant reminders that, here, you weren’t seen as a person anymore. You were just another unit in this massive, impersonal machine.
The very language used in the camp hammered this point home. Orders were always barked in German—a language most prisoners didn’t even understand. But getting those orders right? That was a matter of survival. If you didn’t react quickly enough, punishment was swift and usually came without explanation. Guards hardly ever used names. Instead, they called out numbers or hurled insults. And over time, even the prisoners started doing the same, calling themselves by their assigned numbers—as if their old lives, their real identities, had vanished along with their clothes and belongings.
Hunger and exhaustion took a toll on the body, but it was the relentless humiliation that truly wore people down. Even the simplest things—like using the latrine or washing up—became public, stripped of any privacy or dignity. The camp’s routines kept everyone on edge, never letting anyone feel safe or even remotely normal. And the weather? It seemed to pile on, with brutal winters and oppressive summers making life even harder.
Still, even in this system built to erase humanity, people found ways to hold on. Some clung to memories—a favorite poem, a quiet prayer, or just the stubborn refusal to let go of hope. Others created tiny rituals, like saving a crumb of bread for a friend, or marking the days with a scratch on the wall. These little acts might seem small, but in a place determined to erase you, they were lifelines.
The camp’s hierarchy brought another layer of complexity. Some prisoners got roles as block leaders, work supervisors, or kitchen helpers. Sure, these positions came with tiny privileges, but they also forced people into tough choices. Some went along with the system just to survive, enforcing the rules or looking the other way when others suffered. But there were those who tried to help, quietly smuggling food or offering comfort. The line between victim and perpetrator got blurry, and the camp made it nearly impossible to stay untouched by its cruelty.
For most, the real battle wasn’t physical—it was psychological. The constant pressure to fit in, to obey, to survive no matter what, slowly chipped away at even the strongest spirits. Some prisoners withdrew, becoming numb to everything around them. Others lashed out, turning their frustration on those even weaker. The camp brought out both the best and the worst in people, and nobody left unchanged.
